topics.title: Questions like 去不去 qù bu qù
topics.summary: Say the verb, then bù and the verb again: "go or not go?"
topics.pattern: Subject + Verb + 不 bu + Verb (+ Object)?
text: Another way to ask a yes/no question is to offer both answers: nǐ qù bu qù? Are you going (or not)? It means the same as nǐ qù ma? but sounds more direct and is very common in speech.
The middle bù is said lightly, in the neutral tone. It works with adjectives too: hǎo bu hǎo? is it good? and with shì: nǐ shì bu shì Zhōngguórén?
For yǒu it's yǒu méiyǒu: nǐ yǒu méiyǒu shíjiān? Never add ma to this kind of question: it already is one.

topics.title: 了 le after a verb: it happened
topics.summary: Verb + le says an action is done.
text: le right after a verb marks the action as completed: wǒ mǎile yì běn shū, I bought a book. It isn't a past tense: it can be about the future too (míngtiān xiàle kè wǒ qù zhǎo nǐ, tomorrow when class has finished I'll come and find you).

With a plain object, a sentence like wǒ chīle fàn sounds unfinished. Give the object an amount or description (chīle liǎng wǎn fàn), or add a second le at the end, or keep going: wǒ chīle fàn jiù zǒu, after eating I'll leave.
Habits and states don't take le, even in the past: yǐqián wǒ chángcháng qù, I used to go often. The negative is méi + verb, without le.

topics.title: 了 le at the end: now it's different
topics.summary: Sentence-final le says something has changed or is now the case.
text: At the end of a sentence le announces a new situation: xià yǔ le, it's started raining. Wǒ èr shí wǔ suì le, I'm 25 now. Tiān hēi le, it's got dark.
With bù it means "not any more" or a change of plan: wǒ bù qù le, I'm not going after all. Wǒ bù è le, I'm not hungry any more.
kuài … le and yào … le mean "about to": kuài xià yǔ le, it's about to rain. tài … le is "too, so": tài guì le, too expensive!

topics.title: 过 guo: ever done it
topics.summary: Verb + guo: you have the experience of doing it.
text: guo after a verb says you have done something at some point, as an experience: wǒ qùguo Běijīng, I've been to Beijing. It's the "have you ever …?" of Chinese.
The negative is méi + verb + guo: wǒ méi chīguo Běijīng kǎoyā, I've never had Peking duck. Here guo stays (unlike le).
Ask with ma or with … guo méiyǒu: nǐ qùguo Zhōngguó ma? / nǐ qùguo Zhōngguó méiyǒu?

topics.title: 在 zài, 正在 zhèngzài: doing it right now
topics.summary: zài before a verb: in the middle of doing it.
text: zài before a verb means the action is going on: wǒ zài chīfàn, I'm eating. zhèngzài stresses "right now". ne at the end adds the same idea and is very common in speech: wǒ chīfàn ne.
This is the same zài as "at" a place, now used as "in the middle of". Both can combine: wǒ zài jiā kàn diànshì, I'm watching TV at home (or I watch TV at home).
The negative is méi (zài): wǒ méi zài shuìjiào, I'm not sleeping.

他/tā 正在/zhèngzài 开会/kāihuì 。

topics.title: 想 xiǎng, 要 yào, 会 huì: want and will
topics.summary: xiǎng would like, yào want/going to, huì will (likely).
topics.pattern: Subject + 想 xiǎng / 要 yào / 会 huì + Verb
text: xiǎng + verb is "would like to", soft and polite: wǒ xiǎng qù Zhōngguó. yào + verb is a firmer "want to" or "am going to": wǒ yào qù, I'm going. On its own with a noun, yào means "want" (wǒ yào zhège).
huì + verb predicts: míngtiān huì xià yǔ, it will rain tomorrow. (huì also means "can" for skills: next topic.)
Negatives: bù xiǎng, I don't want to. "Don't want" with yào is usually bù xiǎng, because bú yào means "don't!": bú yào zǒu, don't go.

examples.t: 我/wǒ 想/xiǎng 喝/hē 点儿/diǎnr 水/shuǐ 。
我/wǒ 明年/míngnián 要/yào 去/qù 中国/Zhōngguó 。

topics.title: 能 néng, 会 huì, 可以 kěyǐ: can
topics.summary: huì a learned skill, néng able to, kěyǐ allowed to.
topics.pattern: Subject + 会 huì / 能 néng / 可以 kěyǐ + Verb
text: huì is "can" for skills you learned: wǒ huì shuō Zhōngwén, I can speak Chinese; tā bú huì kāichē, he can't drive.
néng is being able to, given the circumstances: wǒ jīntiān bù néng lái, I can't come today. Also for capacity: tā néng hē shí píng píjiǔ.
kěyǐ is permission: wǒ kěyǐ jìnlái ma? May I come in? Zhèr bù kěyǐ chōuyān, no smoking here. In questions néng and kěyǐ often overlap.

examples.t: 我/wǒ 会/huì 游泳/yóuyǒng 。

topics.title: Comparing with 比 bǐ
topics.summary: A bǐ B + adjective: A is more … than B.
topics.pattern: A + 比 bǐ + B + Adjective (+ difference)
text: tā bǐ wǒ gāo, he is taller than me ("he compared-to me tall"). No hěn here: tā bǐ wǒ hěn gāo is wrong. To say "much taller" add duō le or de duō after it: tā bǐ wǒ gāo duō le.
The difference goes at the end: tā bǐ wǒ dà liǎng suì, she's two years older than me. A little: yìdiǎnr: zhège bǐ nàge guì yìdiǎnr.
"Not as … as" is méiyǒu: wǒ méiyǒu tā gāo, I'm not as tall as him. "The same as" is gēn … yíyàng: wǒ gēn nǐ yíyàng dà, I'm as old as you.

今天/jīntiān 比/bǐ 昨天/zuótiān 冷/lěng 多/duō 了/le 。
examples.en: Today is much colder than yesterday.

topics.title: 得 de: how well something is done
topics.summary: Verb + de + description says how an action is done.
text: To say how someone does something, put de after the verb and the description after it: tā pǎo de hěn kuài, he runs fast. Nǐ shuō de hěn hǎo, you speak well.
With an object, say the verb twice or put the object first: tā shuō Zhōngwén shuō de hěn hǎo, or tā Zhōngwén shuō de hěn hǎo. Never put the object between de and the adjective.

Three de, one sound: 的 before a noun (wǒ de shū), 得 after a verb (shuō de hǎo), and 地 before a verb (mànmān de zǒu, walk slowly). In speech they sound the same; in writing the character tells them apart.

examples.t: 他/tā 跑/pǎo 得/de 很/hěn 快/kuài 。
你/nǐ 中文/Zhōngwén 说/shuō 得/de 很/hěn 好/hǎo 。
我/wǒ 昨天/zuótiān 睡/shuì 得/de 不/bù 好/hǎo 。
examples.en: I didn't sleep well last night.

examples.t: 她/tā 做/zuò 菜/cài 做/zuò 得/de 非常/fēicháng 好吃/hǎochī 。
请/qǐng 慢慢/mànmàn 地/de 说/shuō 。

mistakes.wrong: 他/tā 说/shuō 得/de 中文/Zhōngwén 很/hěn 好/hǎo 。
mistakes.right: 他/tā 中文/Zhōngwén 说/shuō 得/de 很/hěn 好/hǎo 。

mistakes.right: 他/tā 唱/chàng 得/de 很/hěn 好/hǎo 。

他/tā 走/zǒu _ 很/hěn 慢/màn 。

他/tā 高兴/gāoxìng _ 笑/xiào 了/le 。

options: 她/tā 跳舞/tiàowǔ 跳/tiào 得/de 很/hěn 好/hǎo 。
她/tā 跳/tiào 得/de 舞/wǔ 很/hěn 好/hǎo 。
exercises.why: Repeat the verb (or put the object first) before de.

topics.title: How long: duration after the verb
topics.summary: "I studied for two years" puts the time span after the verb.
text: A point in time (zuótiān, sān diǎn) goes before the verb, but a length of time goes after it: wǒ xuéle liǎng nián, I studied for two years. Tā shuìle bā ge xiǎoshí, she slept eight hours.
With an object, either repeat the verb (wǒ xué Zhōngwén xuéle liǎng nián) or put the duration between verb and object with an optional de: wǒ xuéle liǎng nián (de) Zhōngwén.
If it's still going on, add le at the end too: wǒ xué Zhōngwén xuéle liǎng nián le, I've been studying Chinese for two years (and still am).

examples.t: 我/wǒ 等/děng 了/le 二十/èrshí 分钟/fēnzhōng 。
她/tā 睡/shuì 了/le 八/bā 个/ge 小时/xiǎoshí 。

topics.title: "Or": 还是 háishi and 或者 huòzhě
topics.summary: háishi in questions (A or B?), huòzhě in statements (A or B is fine).
topics.pattern: A 还是 háishi B? · A 或者 huòzhě B
text: When you ask someone to choose, use háishi: nǐ hē chá háishi kāfēi? Tea or coffee? The question is in háishi itself, so no ma.
In a statement, "or" is huòzhě: wǒ míngtiān huòzhě hòutiān qù, I'll go tomorrow or the day after. Either is fine.
háishi can also link whole verbs: nǐ qù háishi bú qù? Are you going or not?

examples.t: 你/nǐ 喝/hē 茶/chá 还是/háishi 咖啡/kāfēi ？
examples.en: Would you like tea or coffee?

examples.t: 你/nǐ 是/shì 学生/xuésheng 还是/háishi 老师/lǎoshī ？
